name: hashing/binding-and-scope
about: The two hashes a shared idempotency store makes cross-runtime: the scope a record is kept under, and the binding that says which command it answers. Servers of different implementations sharing one table must agree on both, or each answers the other's retries with already_exists instead of the first attempt's result - a fleet that looks healthy and quietly runs commands twice.
source: spec 12 §4.2 for the two hashes, spec 01 §9 for canonical JSON, and the numbers/ area for the number form. Each digest below was taken over the canonical text in the same case with a general-purpose SHA-256, not read out of a runtime.
rule: binding = SHA-256, lower-case hex, of the canonical JSON of { "op": <operation name>, "args": <coerced arguments> }.
scope = the same hash, of the viewer.
In both, a number is written as ECMAScript writes it (numbers/), so 2.50 and 2.5 are one number and hash alike.
Elsewhere canonical JSON keeps a number as it was written: an implementation that normalises only here changes none of its other hashes.

bindings.name: an operation and its arguments
bindings.why: keys sort at every level: args before op, and id before qty inside it

bindings.name: the same command with the arguments written in another order
bindings.why: same binding: a client that serialises its arguments differently must still get its own retry replayed

bindings.name: nested arguments take the number rule too
bindings.why: 1.0 is the number 1, at any depth

scopes.name: the same viewer with the members in another order
scopes.why: one viewer, one scope, however the server that holds it spells it

scopes.name: no viewer at all
scopes.why: the scope still exists as a value; a keyed command from an anonymous caller is refused for a different reason (§4.1)
